prompt: Properties of algorithms — which statement is correct?
options: Determiniertheit requires that the same input always produces the exact same sequence of intermediate states.
Determinismus requires that the same input always produces the exact same sequence of intermediate states.
Terminierbarkeit requires that the description of the algorithm itself has finite length.
Effektivität requires that an algorithm works for a whole class of inputs, not just one special case.
explanation: Determinismus is the sharpened form: identical input ⇒ identical *steps*. Determiniertheit only demands identical *output*. Terminierbarkeit is halting in finite time (finite *description* is Finitheit), and working for a whole input class is Allgemeinheit (Effektivität = every step is machine-executable).

prompt: Definitions of algorithm properties — which two statements are correct?
options: An algorithm terminates if, for every input, it performs only finitely many steps and then produces an output.
An algorithm is correct if it terminates for every input, regardless of what it outputs.
Every deterministic algorithm is also determiniert.
Every determinierte algorithm is also deterministic.
explanation: Termination = finitely many steps then an output ✓. Correctness is about the output matching the specification — termination alone is not enough ✗. Determinismus (same steps) is strictly stronger than Determiniertheit (same output), so deterministic ⇒ determiniert ✓, but not the reverse ✗ (two different step sequences can reach the same output).

prompt: Loop invariants — which two statements are correct?
options: A loop-invariant proof consists of initialization, maintenance and termination.
A loop invariant must hold before the first iteration and after every iteration of the loop.
A valid loop invariant on its own already proves that the loop terminates.
A loop invariant is only needed for recursive algorithms, not for iterative ones.
explanation: The three-part skeleton is initialization / maintenance / termination ✓, and the invariant must hold before the first and after every iteration ✓. It does *not* prove termination — that is a separate argument (usually a strictly decreasing measure) ✗. And loop invariants are specifically the tool for *iterative* algorithms; recursion is proven by induction ✗.

prompt: Consider `Minimum(A)`: `min = A[0]; for i = 1 to len-1: if A[i] < min then min = A[i]; return min`. Which two statements are correct?
options: The invariant "before iteration i, min is the minimum of A[0..i-1]" holds.
The invariant "before iteration i, min is the minimum of A[0..i]" holds.
At loop exit (i = len) the invariant implies min is the minimum of the whole array.
The invariant only holds if A contains pairwise distinct values.
explanation: The prefix already *processed* before iteration i is A[0..i-1] ✓ — A[i] has not been compared yet, so option 2 is off by one ✗. Substituting i = len into the invariant gives exactly the postcondition ✓. Duplicates are irrelevant: `<` simply leaves min unchanged on ties ✗.

prompt: `MaxIndex(A)` returns the largest idx such that every element of A[1..idx] is less than double its predecessor, using a latching flag `conditionTrue`. Which two statements are correct?
options: Without the latching flag the algorithm could return an index that lies after a violation of the run condition.
The flag is only a performance optimization; removing it never changes the returned value.
Once the run condition fails, the flag must stay false for all remaining iterations.
The invariant can be stated purely in terms of idx, without mentioning conditionTrue.
explanation: A single violation invalidates *every* later index, not just the violating one — so without latching, a later element that happens to satisfy the condition would wrongly overwrite idx ✓✗. Latching (staying false forever) is exactly what makes this a genuine invariant ✓, and the invariant therefore has to mention the flag ✗.

prompt: Reasons to deliberately choose a *less* efficient algorithm — which two statements are correct?
options: A constant-time algorithm may be preferred because runtime itself can leak secret information through a timing side-channel.
A simpler but slower algorithm may be preferred because it is easier to verify formally.
It is never legitimate — the asymptotically fastest algorithm is always the correct choice.
Compilers automatically rewrite inefficient code into efficient code, so the choice is irrelevant.
explanation: Both timing side-channels ✓ and ease of formal verification ✓ are listed in the lecture as legitimate reasons. Parallelizability and code/silicon size are two more. Options 3 and 4 are simply false — asymptotics is one resource among several (time variance, memory, energy, size, kind of operation), and no compiler changes an algorithm's asymptotic class for you.

prompt: Abstract data types (ADTs) — which two statements are correct?
options: An ADT describes possible values, operations and behaviour of a data type, but not its concrete implementation.
The ADT description specifies the time complexity of the operations.
The same ADT can be realised by several different data structures with different runtimes.
Two data structures implementing the same ADT must have the same asymptotic runtimes.
explanation: An ADT is a purely behavioural contract ✓ — it deliberately says nothing about complexity ✗. That is why one ADT (e.g. "List") has many realisations ✓ (array vs. linked list) whose runtimes differ substantially ✗.

prompt: Correctness proof of an in-place sorting algorithm — which two statements are correct?
options: Besides sortedness, one must show the permutation property: the algorithm only rearranges values, never invents or drops one.
Sortedness of the output alone is sufficient to prove a sorting algorithm correct.
Termination has to be shown separately, e.g. via a quantity that strictly decreases toward a bound.
For an in-place algorithm the permutation property follows automatically from termination.
explanation: The three-part standard argument is termination ✓, sortedness, and the permutation property ✓. Sortedness alone is not enough ✗ — an "algorithm" that outputs [0,0,...,0] is sorted but wrong. And nothing about halting implies values were preserved ✗.

prompt: Berechenbarkeit (computability) criteria — which two statements are correct?
options: Finitheit: the description of the algorithm has finite length.
Effektivität: every single step is actually executable on a machine.
Finitheit: the algorithm halts after finitely many steps on every input.
Effektivität: the algorithm is the fastest known solution for the problem.
explanation: Berechenbarkeit splits into Finitheit (finite *description*) ✓, Terminierbarkeit (finite *execution* — that is what option 3 describes) ✗ and Effektivität (each step machine-executable) ✓. Effektivität has nothing to do with being the fastest known algorithm ✗ — that is Effizienz.
